difficultyRationale: Requires knowing why the Spring team recommends constructor injection beyond style — the fail-fast startup behavior is the part candidates often can't articulate.
prompt: A service class has three dependencies wired with `@Autowired` directly on the fields. A teammate proposes switching to constructor injection with no `@Autowired` annotation needed (a single constructor). Besides making the class easier to unit test without a Spring context, what concrete behavioral difference does this change introduce at application startup if two beans end up depending on each other?
explanation: With field injection, Spring can instantiate a bean (via its no-arg constructor) before any of its dependencies are injected, so a circular dependency between two singleton beans can often be silently resolved by injecting an early, partially-initialized reference. With constructor injection, a bean cannot be instantiated at all until every constructor argument is available, so a genuine circular dependency between two constructor-injected beans fails the application context at startup with a `BeanCurrentlyInCreationException`, rather than succeeding with a partially-constructed object graph.

options.text: There is no behavioral difference; both forms fail at startup identically if a cycle exists, since Spring resolves every `@Autowired` injection point, whether on a field or a constructor parameter, during one unified instantiation phase before the bean is handed back to the container.
options.explanation: Field injection and constructor injection differ precisely in when the bean is considered fully constructed relative to dependency resolution, which changes whether a cycle is tolerated or rejected.

options.text: Constructor injection makes a circular dependency fail fast at startup with a clear error, whereas field injection can silently succeed by injecting a not-yet-fully-initialized bean into the cycle.
options.explanation: Correct. Field-injected (and setter-injected) beans can be constructed via their default constructor and registered as 'currently in creation' before their fields are populated, letting the container hand out an early reference to break the cycle. Constructor injection requires every argument up front, so Spring cannot do this and raises `BeanCurrentlyInCreationException` instead.

options.text: Constructor injection disables Spring's circular dependency detection entirely, so a cycle between two constructor-injected beans goes unnoticed at startup and only surfaces much later as a NullPointerException once the half-wired object is actually used in production.
options.explanation: This is backwards: constructor injection is what makes Spring detect and reject the cycle immediately, rather than letting it through.

options.text: Field injection throws at startup for any cycle between two singleton beans, while constructor injection automatically resolves the same cycle by substituting a lazy proxy for one of the two dependencies, with no extra configuration required.
options.explanation: No proxy is automatically introduced for a plain singleton cycle, and it is field/setter injection — not constructor injection — that can quietly let a cycle through.
